intro_1: This is Forja, the programming environment of Dash for the Amiga. A lot has changed since the first video.
intro_2: I will install it on CoffinOS and go through all of it. A more comfortable editor, the Dash help, a complete debugger, git, an AI copilot, tools to make demos, a window designer and a 3D editor.
instalar_1: Forja comes inside the Dash package. This is version 2.20, which is not published yet.
instalar_2: I unpack it with LhA into RAM, and the installer updates the Dash this Amiga already had.
instalar_3: When it finishes, I open the Dash drawer. Forja is inside.
proyecto_1: Forja works with projects: a drawer with a dot forja file. It is created from a template. There are six: Shell command, commodity, MUI application, game, demo and 3D.
proyecto_2: I pick the game one. It already comes with a program that builds and starts.
editor_1: The editor colours the whole language. On the left are the project files, and below is the output.
editor_2: I will write a function. When I open a parenthesis or quotes, Forja adds the closing one. And a func brings its own end.
editor_3: In the Editor menu there is comment a line. Control D duplicates it, and Control Alt with the arrows moves it up or down.
editor_4: Control O opens the outline of the file, with its functions and constants. Typing filters it.
editor_5: Control T goes to a name anywhere in the project, whatever file it is in.
editor_6: Control Shift F searches the whole project. The results show below, and a click goes to each one.
editor_7: F4 folds a block, to see the file shorter.
ayuda_1: F1 on a name opens its page in the Dash help. It has the signature, what it does and an example with colours.
ayuda_2: You can also search by words. I type rect and the pages that have it show up.
ayuda_3: The Try button opens the example of the page in a new tab and runs it, without leaving Forja.
errores_1: When I save, Forja checks the program in the background. Here I get a function name wrong. The error is marked on its line, and also below.
errores_2: F8 jumps to the next error. I delete the line, save, and the warning goes away.
errores_3: Build is Amiga K and run is Amiga E. Building takes a tenth of a second.
errores_4: And here is the game from the template, with its hardware sprite.
depurar_1: For the debugger I use a small program that adds one to ten. I set a breakpoint on the line with the sum, with F9.
depurar_2: And I give it a condition: stop only when i is seven. It is typed in a question above the editor.
depurar_3: When debugging, it stops where it should. On the left are the stack and the variables. I can watch an expression, for example total times two.
depurar_4: With the pointer over a name, its value shows. And with the program stopped I can change a variable: total, one hundred.
depurar_5: I continue, and the program uses the new value. The sum gives one hundred and thirty-four.
git_1: Git is an extension that uses dashgit. This project already has a repository, and its branch is on the right of the bar.
git_2: When I type, the bar counts the changes. The project panel marks the file with an M, and the editor margin puts a stripe on the new line.
git_3: The Changes panel lists the files. I tick the file, and with two clicks I see its differences, in colours.
git_4: I type the message and Return commits. The commit is done, and the bar no longer counts changes.
inferencia_1: Inferencia is the AI of the Amiga, and Forja uses it as a copilot. Note that in this demonstration there is no real model. A test server answers, with replies written in advance.
inferencia_2: Change the code: I ask for the scoreboard to show the lives too. The change arrives as a view of differences: in red what it removes, in green what it adds.
inferencia_3: I accept it with the a key, and it is applied in the editor. Amiga Z undoes it.
inferencia_4: Write the test creates a new file with a test program. When I accept it, Forja runs it and counts the checks: two good, zero bad.
inferencia_5: If the compiler gives an error, Explain the error tells it in the Inferencia window.
inferencia_6: And Fix the error proposes the correction, again with its view of differences.
sprites_1: Sprites and maps are two extensions, and they do not load if you only program. With Amiga B I create a new BOB.
sprites_2: I draw with the pencil, the line, the box and the fill, and I make a second frame to animate it.
sprites_3: The map editor uses a BOB as the tileset. I paint the ground and a platform, and the game loads it with tilemap load.
demos_1: For making demos there is another extension, and a template. It brings its screen, the loop of each frame and an asm block that paints colour bars, line by line.
demos_2: The asm ... end block has its own colours: instructions, registers and labels.
demos_3: With the demo running, the Demos window connects by itself. The sync tracks are values that change with the music, as in Rocket.
demos_4: I change a key in the table and the demo gets it right away. Here the speed of the bar changes.
demos_5: The MOD viewer shows the patterns of the module, with the row that is playing highlighted.
demos_6: The copper editor makes gradients and per-line changes, and tries them for real on a screen.
demos_7: The raster meter tells how many lines each frame uses: green, yellow and red as it gets close to the limit.
demos_8: And Parts puts on a timeline which scene goes from which row to which row of the music.
tresd_1: With the 3D template and MiniGL, a cube spins with the gl functions. It needs an FPU, and the project already builds with it.
ventanas_1: Now, the window designer, like the one in Visual Basic or Delphi. Jose asked for it in the Dash group. With it I will make a task list, starting from the MUI template.
ventanas_2: The window is drawn as MUI will lay it out. The palette of objects is above, and on the right, the properties of the one I pick. I remove the row of buttons of the template.
ventanas_3: I drag a button from the palette next to the field. A line shows where it will land. Below, with a click on the palette and another on the window, I put a list and another button.
ventanas_4: Objects move with the mouse: I take the text at the top to the end, so it becomes the status line.
ventanas_5: In the properties I change the texts: Task, Add, Delete and No tasks.
ventanas_6: Now the events. A double click on Add: Forja gives it a number and a name, and in main dot dash it makes its if. I write what it does: the text of the field goes into the list.
ventanas_7: I give the field the same event number, so Return adds too. The list tells when a line is picked, and I show it below. And Delete removes the picked one.
ventanas_8: I run it with Amiga E. I add two tasks, one with the button and one with Return, pick one, and delete it. All with a few lines. The Dash extension for VS Code does the same.
taller_1: And the last one: the 3D Workshop, an extension for Titan Force, the 3D game we are making in Dash. It edits the models, their bones, the animations and the scene. The robot is by SantiDarkG.
taller_2: I open the robot from the project. Dragging with the mouse turns the camera around it.
taller_3: Key 2 switches to the animations. I pick an arm bone with the arrows and turn it with Q: that is how a key pose is made. Space plays the whole punch.
taller_4: Key 3 shows the neighbourhood scene from above. N puts in a new house, and I drag it into place.
taller_5: Amiga S saves to files the game reads as they are: the animations and the scene show up in the project.
cierre_1: Git, Inferencia, Sprites, Maps, Demos and the 3D Workshop are extensions. The extension manager turns them on, turns them off and installs them.
cierre_2: Forja and Dash are free. They are on GitHub, under FreeMEM.
